text: Lesson 10 reconstructed the timeline: phishing email, initial access, lateral movement, data staging. Once that sequence is understood, scoping asks the next question - systematically checking everything else the attacker might have touched, beyond the entities that already showed up in the timeline. Scoping isn't a vague worry about further damage; it's a defined, repeatable check.

Scoping breaks into three concrete checks. What other accounts did the attacker access using the credentials or sessions they already had. What other hosts did they connect to beyond the ones already identified, directly or through lateral movement. And did any data actually leave the environment, not just sit somewhere the attacker theoretically could have reached it.

Take the account compromised at 9:02am and used for lateral movement at 9:15am. Scoping means checking that account's full sign-in history across the whole incident window, not just the one sign-in already found. That check turns up a second sign-in at 9:28am to a different application using single sign-on - a host the original timeline never surfaced on its own, because nobody had gone looking for it yet.

A very common real failure is fixing what was found and declaring the incident closed without checking for a second foothold. Resetting the compromised password and rebuilding the file server fixes what the team found. If that second SSO sign-in never gets checked, the attacker may still hold a valid session or a persistence mechanism elsewhere, and the incident reopens days later looking like a brand-new case instead of the same attacker returning.

A properly scoped incident can answer three questions with evidence, not assumption: every account touched has been checked, every host reached has been checked, and any data the attacker could access has been checked for actual exfiltration. Getting that right, before anyone calls the incident closed, is what Lesson 12's severity classification, and Chapter 4's containment decisions, both depend on.
